questions.stem:
On a topographical map of scale 1:50,000, a footpath runs from a trigonometrical station at 620 m to a bridge at 380 m. The footpath measures 9.6 cm on the map, and a woodland covers 36 complete grid squares, each 1 cm by 1 cm.
(a) Calculate the length of the footpath on the ground in kilometres. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the average gradient of the footpath. [4 marks]
(c) Calculate the area of the woodland in km². [3 marks]
(d) Describe how relief is shown on topographical maps by any three methods other than contours. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: 9.6 x 50,000 = 480,000 cm = 4.8 km
4 marks: VI = 620 - 380 = 240 m; HE = 4,800 m; gradient = 240/4,800 = 1 in 20
3 marks: each square = 0.5 km x 0.5 km = 0.25 km²; 36 x 0.25 = 9 km²
5 marks: any three described (2,2,1) - spot heights (dots with heights); trigonometrical stations (triangles with heights); hachures (short lines in direction of slope); hill shading; layer tinting (colours for height bands); form lines
questions.explanation: Model answer: (a) 9.6 cm x 50,000 = 4.8 km. (b) Vertical interval 240 m over 4,800 m gives 1 in 20. (c) 36 squares of 0.25 km² = 9 km². (d) Relief may also be shown by spot heights, trigonometrical stations, hachures, hill shading and layer colouring.

questions.stem:
The table shows the output of crops from a farm settlement in tonnes: Maize 120, Cassava 90, Yam 60, Rice 30. Total 300.
(a) Calculate the angle of the sector for each crop in a pie chart. [8 marks]
(b) State two advantages and one disadvantage of the pie chart as a method of data presentation. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: maize 120/300 x 360 = 144°
2 marks: cassava 90/300 x 360 = 108°
2 marks: yam 60/300 x 360 = 72°
2 marks: rice 30/300 x 360 = 36°
3 marks: first advantage - shows proportions of a whole clearly / easy to read
2 marks: second advantage - visually attractive / easy to compare components
2 marks: disadvantage - difficult to read small sectors / unsuitable for many components / absolute values not shown
questions.explanation: Model answer: Maize 144°, cassava 108°, yam 72°, rice 36° (total 360°). Pie charts show parts of a whole clearly and are attractive, but small sectors are hard to compare and actual quantities are not shown without labels.

questions.stem:
(a) Define GIS. [3 marks]
(b) Explain the role of hardware, software, data, people and methods in a GIS. [7 marks]
(c) Give five examples of how GIS can help a state government in Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: a computer-based system for capturing, storing, analysing, managing and displaying spatially referenced data
7 marks: components - hardware (2), software (2), data (1), people/users (1), methods/procedures (1)
5 marks: any five, 1 mark each - urban planning; mapping flood-prone areas; census and electoral mapping; locating facilities; agriculture/crop monitoring; security and crime mapping; transport route planning
questions.explanation: Model answer: GIS is a computer system that captures, stores, analyses and displays data linked to location. Its components are hardware, software, data, people and methods. In Nigeria it is used for town planning, flood mapping, census and electoral mapping, siting facilities, crop monitoring and security.

questions.stem:
(a) With reference to the rotation of the earth, explain three effects of rotation. [9 marks]
(b) Town A is on longitude 15°E and Town B is on longitude 60°W. When it is 2:00 p.m. at Town A, what is the local time at Town B? Show your working. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: day and night - the half facing the sun has day
3 marks: deflection of winds and ocean currents (Coriolis force) - right in N. hemisphere, left in S.
3 marks: time differences between places - 4 minutes per degree of longitude; or daily rise and fall of tides; or flattening at poles
2 marks: difference in longitude = 15 + 60 = 75°
2 marks: time difference = 75 x 4 minutes = 300 minutes = 5 hours
2 marks: B is west, so behind A: 2:00 p.m. - 5 h = 9:00 a.m.
questions.explanation: Model answer: Rotation causes day and night, the deflection of winds and currents, and differences in local time of four minutes per degree of longitude. Towns A and B are 75° apart, a difference of 5 hours; B, being west, is behind, so when A reads 2:00 p.m., B reads 9:00 a.m.

questions.stem:
(a) With the aid of description, explain how a rift valley is formed. [8 marks]
(b) Describe two other landforms produced by faulting. [4 marks]
(c) State three economic importance of mountains. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: tensional forces in the crust produce two roughly parallel normal faults
3 marks: the central block between the faults sinks (or the sides rise), creating a long, narrow, steep-sided depression
3 marks: example - East African Rift Valley/Jordan valley; steep fault scarps on either side; floor may contain lakes
4 marks: any two, 2 marks each - block mountain/horst (uplifted block between faults); fault scarp/escarpment; tilt block
3 marks: any three, 1 mark each - tourism; minerals; sources of rivers/HEP; climate barrier/rain; forestry; grazing
questions.explanation: Model answer: Tension stretches the crust and produces parallel normal faults; the block between them subsides to form a steep-sided rift valley such as the East African Rift. Faulting also produces horsts (block mountains) and fault scarps. Mountains support tourism, mining, HEP from their rivers, forestry and grazing.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the processes of river erosion. [8 marks]
(b) Explain how the following are formed: (i) a waterfall (ii) a meander. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: hydraulic action - force of moving water loosens and removes material
2 marks: corrasion/abrasion - load grinds against bed and banks
2 marks: attrition - particles collide and break into smaller, rounder pieces
2 marks: corrosion/solution - chemical dissolving of soluble rocks such as limestone
4 marks: waterfall - river flows over hard rock lying on soft rock; soft rock eroded faster, creating a step; plunge pool undercuts, hard cap collapses and the fall retreats upstream forming a gorge
3 marks: meander - faster flow on the outer bank erodes a river cliff while slower flow on the inner bank deposits a slip-off slope, increasing the bend
questions.explanation: Model answer: Rivers erode by hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution. A waterfall forms where hard rock overlies softer rock: the soft rock is cut back, a plunge pool deepens and the overhang collapses, so the fall retreats. A meander develops as the outer bank is eroded and the inner bank receives deposits.

questions.stem:
The table shows the mean monthly rainfall (mm) of a station in Nigeria from January to December: 10, 25, 80, 140, 180, 220, 260, 240, 200, 120, 30, 5.
(a) Calculate the total annual rainfall. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the annual range of rainfall. [3 marks]
(c) How many months have 50 mm of rainfall or more? [3 marks]
(d) Describe two features of the rainfall regime shown. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: 10+25+80+140+180+220+260+240+200+120+30+5 = 1,510 mm
3 marks: 260 - 5 = 255 mm
3 marks: March to October = 8 months
3 marks: one rainy season with a peak in July (single maximum)
3 marks: dry season from November to February with very little rain (harmattan period)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Total 1,510 mm; range 260 - 5 = 255 mm; eight months (March-October) have at least 50 mm. The station has a single rainy season peaking in July and a marked dry season from November to February, typical of the Guinea savanna.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain how altitude and distance from the sea influence temperature. [8 marks]
(b) A station at sea level records 30°C. Using a lapse rate of 6.5°C per 1,000 m, calculate the expected temperature at the top of a mountain 2,000 m high. [4 marks]
(c) Name three instruments used to measure elements of weather and state what each measures. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: altitude - temperature falls with height (about 6.5°C per 1,000 m) because air is thinner and heated mainly from the ground
4 marks: distance from the sea - coastal areas have smaller ranges because the sea heats and cools slowly; interiors have greater ranges (continentality)
4 marks: 2 x 6.5 = 13°C fall; 30 - 13 = 17°C
3 marks: any three, 1 mark each - thermometer (temperature); barometer (pressure); rain gauge (rainfall); anemometer (wind speed); wind vane (direction); hygrometer (humidity)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Temperature drops by about 6.5°C per 1,000 m; coastal places have moderate ranges while interior places have extreme ranges. At 2,000 m the temperature is 30 - 13 = 17°C. Instruments include the thermometer, barometer and rain gauge.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain four causes of desertification in northern Nigeria. [12 marks]
(b) Suggest four measures to control desertification. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: any four causes, 3 marks each - low and unreliable rainfall/drought; overgrazing; deforestation for fuelwood; bush burning; over-cultivation/continuous cropping; population pressure; climate change
8 marks: any four measures, 2 marks each - afforestation and shelter belts (Great Green Wall); controlled grazing/ranching; alternative fuels; irrigation; education; legislation against bush burning; improved farming methods
questions.explanation: Model answer: Desertification results from erratic rainfall and drought made worse by overgrazing, felling trees for fuelwood, bush burning, over-cultivation and rising population. It can be checked by tree planting and shelter belts such as the Great Green Wall, controlled grazing, alternative fuels, irrigation, education and enforcement of laws.

questions.stem:
(a) Why are some parts of the world crowded while others are almost empty? Explain four reasons. [12 marks]
(b) What problems arise when a country is overpopulated? State four. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: any four factors, 3 marks each - climate; relief; soil fertility; water supply; mineral resources; industrialisation; transport; government policy; historical factors; pests and diseases
8 marks: any four, 2 marks each - unemployment; food shortages; housing shortages/slums; pressure on social amenities; crime; environmental degradation; congestion
questions.explanation: Model answer: People cluster where climate is favourable, land is lowland and fertile, water and minerals are available and industry and transport offer jobs, while harsh deserts, high mountains and disease-ridden areas are sparsely settled. Overpopulation brings unemployment, food and housing shortages, strained amenities, crime and environmental damage.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain four factors that influence the siting of rural settlements. [12 marks]
(b) Describe four functions of urban centres. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: any four, 3 marks each - water supply; fertile land; defence; relief/dry site; route focus; building materials; security; nearness to resources
8 marks: any four, 2 marks each - administrative; commercial; industrial; educational; religious; transport; residential; tourist/recreational
questions.explanation: Model answer: Rural settlements are sited near water, on fertile land, on defensible or dry sites, at route junctions and near building materials. Towns serve administrative, commercial, industrial, educational, religious, transport and residential functions.

questions.stem:
(a) Compare road and rail transport under four headings. [12 marks]
(b) State four problems of transportation in developing countries. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: any four comparisons, 3 marks each - flexibility (road door-to-door; rail fixed routes); cost for bulky goods over long distances (rail cheaper); speed over short distances (road faster); construction/maintenance cost; safety/accident rate; capacity
8 marks: any four, 2 marks each - poor maintenance; inadequate funds; bad terrain; congestion; old vehicles/rolling stock; insecurity; poor planning; corruption
questions.explanation: Model answer: Roads are flexible and fast over short distances; rail carries bulky goods cheaply over long distances on fixed routes and is safer, though costlier to build. Problems include poor maintenance, lack of funds, difficult terrain, congestion, outdated equipment and insecurity.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five factors that influence the location of industries. [15 marks]
(b) Give five reasons why some industries are located near their markets. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
15 marks: any five, 3 marks each - raw materials; power; labour; market; transport; capital; government policy; water supply; land; historical/inertia
5 marks: any five, 1 mark each - perishable products; bulky/fragile finished goods; weight-gaining industries; need for after-sales service; changing fashions; competition
questions.explanation: Model answer: Industries locate according to raw materials, power, labour, markets, transport, capital, government policy, water and land. Market location suits perishable, bulky, fragile or weight-gaining goods and products needing close contact with customers.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between balance of trade and balance of payments. [6 marks]
(b) Explain four factors that affect international trade. [8 marks]
(c) State three problems of trade among West African countries. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: balance of trade - difference between value of visible exports and visible imports (3); balance of payments - record of all transactions, visible and invisible, including capital flows (3)
8 marks: any four, 2 marks each - differences in resources; differences in climate; levels of technology; demand; transport; government policies/tariffs; exchange rates
6 marks: any three, 2 marks each - similar exports; poor transport; different currencies; tariffs and border restrictions; smuggling; political instability
questions.explanation: Model answer: The balance of trade compares visible exports and imports, whereas the balance of payments includes all transactions with the rest of the world. Trade is shaped by resources, climate, technology, demand, transport, policies and exchange rates. West African trade suffers from similar exports, poor transport, separate currencies, restrictions and instability.

questions.stem:
(a) Identify four conditions that attract tourists to a destination and explain each. [12 marks]
(b) In what four ways does tourism contribute to the economy of a host country? [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: any four, 3 marks each - scenic attractions; cultural/historical sites; good climate; security; accommodation and transport facilities; publicity; government policy
8 marks: any four, 2 marks each - foreign exchange; employment; infrastructure development; revenue; market for local crafts; cultural exchange
questions.explanation: Model answer: Tourism thrives where there are attractive scenery, cultural and historical sites, a pleasant climate, security, good hotels and transport, publicity and supportive policy. It earns foreign exchange, creates jobs, stimulates infrastructure and markets for crafts and raises government revenue.

questions.stem:
(a) Divide Nigeria into its major relief regions and describe each. [12 marks]
(b) Show two ways in which the relief of Nigeria affects economic activities. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: coastal lowlands and the Niger Delta - swamps, lagoons, creeks
3 marks: Niger-Benue troughs and Sokoto/Chad plains - low-lying river basins
3 marks: central/Jos plateau and western uplands - high plateau, inselbergs
3 marks: eastern highlands - Obudu, Mambilla, Gotel (Chappal Waddi)
8 marks: any two, 4 marks each - highlands cool for tourism and temperate crops (Jos, Obudu); rivers from highlands for HEP (Kainji); swamps hinder transport; plains favour farming and settlement
questions.explanation: Model answer: Nigeria has coastal lowlands and the swampy Niger Delta; the Niger-Benue troughs and the Sokoto and Chad plains; the Jos Plateau and western uplands; and the eastern highlands of Obudu, Mambilla and Gotel. Highlands favour tourism and cool-climate crops and feed rivers for HEP, while swamps hinder transport and plains support farming.

questions.stem:
(a) Nigerian farmers face many difficulties. Explain four of them. [12 marks]
(b) What four measures can government take to boost agricultural production in Nigeria? [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: any four, 3 marks each - poor storage/processing; inadequate credit; land tenure system; poor transport; pests and diseases; insecurity/herder-farmer clashes; climate variability; rural-urban migration
8 marks: any four, 2 marks each - provision of credit; mechanisation; improved seeds and fertilisers; extension services; storage facilities; irrigation; security; good feeder roads
questions.explanation: Model answer: Agriculture suffers from poor storage and processing, lack of credit, fragmented land holdings, bad roads, pests, insecurity, unreliable rains and the drift of youth to towns. It can be improved by credit, mechanisation, improved inputs, extension services, storage, irrigation, security and feeder roads.

questions.stem:
(a) Name four solid minerals found in Nigeria and state where each is found. [8 marks]
(b) Explain three problems of the mining industry in Nigeria. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
8 marks: any four mineral-location pairs, 2 marks each - tin (Jos); coal (Enugu); iron ore (Itakpe); limestone (Ewekoro/Obajana); bitumen (Ondo); gold (Zamfara/Osun); lead-zinc (Abakaliki)
12 marks: any three, 4 marks each - illegal mining; environmental degradation; poor infrastructure; inadequate capital/technology; neglect due to oil dependence; insecurity
questions.explanation: Model answer: Nigeria's solid minerals include tin on the Jos Plateau, coal at Enugu, iron ore at Itakpe, limestone at Ewekoro and Obajana and bitumen in Ondo. Mining is hampered by illegal mining, environmental damage, poor infrastructure, lack of capital and technology, neglect in favour of oil and insecurity.

questions.stem:
(a) Outline four goals for which the Economic Community of West African States was set up. [8 marks]
(b) Discuss three challenges that limit the success of ECOWAS today. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
8 marks: any four, 2 marks each - promote economic integration; free movement of people, goods and services; common external tariff; improved living standards; development of infrastructure; peace and security
12 marks: any three, 4 marks each - political instability and coups; withdrawal of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger (2025); language/colonial differences; poor infrastructure; similar exports; non-implementation of protocols; funding problems
questions.explanation: Model answer: ECOWAS aims at economic integration, free movement of people and goods, a common external tariff, better living standards, regional infrastructure and peace. It faces coups and instability, the withdrawal of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, linguistic divisions, poor transport, similar exports and weak implementation.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the stages involved in carrying out a field work on a local market. [12 marks]
(b) State four instruments or materials needed for the field work. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: planning - choice of topic, aims, permission, reconnaissance
3 marks: data collection - observation, questionnaires, interviews, counting, measurement
3 marks: data processing and analysis - tables, graphs, maps
3 marks: report writing - introduction, methods, findings, conclusion and recommendations
8 marks: any four, 2 marks each - notebook/pen; questionnaire; compass; measuring tape; camera; GPS; map of the area
questions.explanation: Model answer: Field work begins with planning and a reconnaissance visit, followed by data collection through observation, questionnaires and counts, then processing of data into tables and maps, and finally a written report. Useful materials include notebooks, questionnaires, a compass, measuring tape, camera and a map.
